I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

The people responsible have faced no consequences
I have lost my connection to my community and culture

vignette:
Aroha Ngata is a twenty-nine-year-old New Zealand Māori woman who relocated to the United States several years ago to pursue a professional dance career. She presented for psychological assessment following a terrorist attack she survived at a crowded public venue approximately fourteen months ago. Her PCL-5 score of 69 places her in the severe range, and her presentation reflects a tightly interlocking set of cognitive and behavioural patterns that have progressively narrowed her world.

The attack unfolded without warning. Aroha had been performing at an outdoor cultural festival when an armed assailant opened fire into the crowd. She was caught in a corridor between two stage barriers - hemmed in on both sides, unable to move, watching people fall around her. The sensation of having no options, of being physically trapped with no exit, became seared into the fabric of the experience. She survived by remaining motionless for nearly forty minutes until the scene was secured. In the weeks that followed, she found she could not construct a coherent account of what had happened. Her memories arrived in disconnected pieces - a flash of a particular colour, the texture of the ground beneath her palms - without narrative sequence or verbal form. She could not put the event into words in any way that felt true to it, and sometimes the full emotional weight of those forty minutes would descend on her without any accompanying image at all, as though the fear had become autonomous. These fractured, nonverbal memory qualities made it impossible to process the event as something past and bounded, and they fed directly into her conviction that the world remained dangerous: if she could not understand what had happened, she could not be sure it would not happen again.

Aroha now works as a dance instructor at a studio in the city, and it is there that the architecture of her symptoms becomes most visible. When a door to the practice room closes behind a group of students, she feels the walls contract. Enclosed or confined spaces - the changing room, the elevator, even a full studio with the blinds drawn - have become intolerable, and she has begun teaching with the studio door propped open regardless of weather or noise complaints, a habit her employer has started to notice. When a student enters mid-session and the door swings shut with a bang, Aroha's body responds before her mind does: her attention locks onto the sound, scanning for what it might mean, and within seconds she is listening for further sounds that might indicate someone entering from another direction. This hypervigilance toward unexpected sounds and toward strangers approaching her - even a parent walking across the floor to collect a child - is not experienced as irrational. She is certain, in those moments, that the threat is real. The heightened state of alert then pulls her back toward the sensory fragments of the attack itself, so that trigger and memory feed one another in a loop she cannot interrupt from the outside.

She has also come to believe that the people responsible for the attack have faced no consequences, and this absence of accountability has hollowed out whatever meaning she once drew from her work and her cultural identity. Dance was, for Aroha, inseparable from her connection to her Māori community and her sense of self; she has lost that thread entirely, and the loss feels permanent. When certain conversation topics arise - anything touching on public safety, political violence, or even the name of the venue - the appraisal that nothing matters and no one is held responsible surges forward, and with it comes a fresh wave of fragmented sensory memory and the feeling of entrapment all over again. To manage this, she has adopted a rigid practice of forcing herself to think only positive thoughts whenever distress rises, and she spends long hours trying to find a reason why this happened to her specifically. But these strategies prevent her from sitting with the memory long enough to integrate it, keeping it raw and unprocessed, which sustains the sense of ongoing threat and confirms, in her mind, that the world is as dangerous as her body insists it is. The positive reframing, in particular, has left her feeling fraudulent and further cut off from her community, deepening the appraisal that she has lost something irretrievable.

What finally brought Aroha to seek help was a session last month in which she found herself unable to enter the studio at all, standing outside for twenty minutes before leaving. She is most afraid that she will never dance again - and most hoping, tentatively, that someone can help her find words for what she cannot yet say.
